newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Delamere in qualified defence of NZ super wording.
newsitem.headline: Delamere in qualified defence of NZ super wording.

text.p: Associate Treasurer Tuariki John Delamere on Tuesday defended the wording of the question to be put to a referendum on compulsory superannuation, but said he would not "die in a ditch for it".
Draft legislation includes the question: "Are you for or against the retirement savings scheme?"
But there has been a unified call from pressure groups to insert the word "compulsory" to make the purpose of the referendum more transparent.
It is widely believed Treasurer Winston Peters pressed for "compulsory" to be omitted.
Answering questions after a breakfast speech to the National Press Club, Delamere said he did not see leaving out "compulsory" as an attempt to make the question less frightening.
"Not from my point of view no. But I wouldn't die in a ditch for it (the current wording)," he said.
He said many things government did imposed a compulsion on people but that was not included in the wording of all laws.
The problem of funding superannuation with an ageing population would persist, he said.
"Whether the popular vote is yes or no (at the referendum), the problem won't go away."
A government-appointed team is designing the shape of the scheme to be put to the referendum and is expected to release a White Paper in July. The referendum will be held in September.
A parliamentary select committee hearing submissions on the referendum legislation will meet again on Tuesday afternoon.
It is expected to insert the word 'compulsory' and make other changes before it reports the bill back to parliament.
